question.leadin: You probably know more about Hawaiian mythology than you think you do.
question.text: The menehune (MEN-eh-HOO-neh) are the Hawaiian equivalents of these little people that, in Norse mythology, make excellent smiths.
question.clue: Orange Alternative claimed there could be "no freedom without" what creatures? These creatures were graffitied in spots where Polish authorities had painted over anti-government messages.

swap.leadin: One of these events in August 1980 was sparked by the firing of Anna Walentynowicz ["VAL-en-TIN-oh-WITCH"].
swap.text: Name this type of action undertaken by workers at the Lenin Shipyards under the leadership of electrical engineer Lech Walesa ["WUH-leh-SUH"]. Arthur Scargill led several of these actions for British coal miners.
swap.answerHtml: strikes [accept labor strikes or strike actions; prompt on protests or walkouts or factory occupations or industrial actions]
swap.clue: The headline "Crisis? What Crisis?" was used to criticize James Callaghan's handling of a wave of these events that became known as the "Winter of Discontent."

question.text: Sigismund II's inability to bear a child resulted in the formation of this personal union partitioned by Prussia, Austria, and Russia. Napoleon later revived a small part of it as the Grand Duchy of Warsaw.
question.clue: Monarchs agreed to the Henrician Articles and made individual commitments called the pacta conventa on becoming rulers of this country.

swap.text: Two answers required. Teuton leader Conrad Zollner von Rothenstein protested a marriage between leaders of these two countries to the Pope. A "commonwealth" created by these two countries was partially formed by the Union of Krakow and Vilnius.
swap.clue: The head of one of these countries instigated Zeligowski's Mutiny in the other.

question.leadin: Answer the following about Eastern European leaders.
question.text: A former mayor of Warsaw, this Polish president died in a plane crash in April 2010 and unfortunately shares his name with the Unabomber.

swap.leadin: Name these Europeans who served in the Continental Army.
swap.text: This Polish military engineer created defenses for the Americans at the Battle of Saratoga. He led a namesake uprising against Russia during the Third Partition of Poland.
swap.clue: This American Revolution veteran issued the Manifesto of Polaniec (POLE-AHN-EE-YETS) and won at Raclawice (RAHTS-WAH-FEE-TSAY) before being defeated at Maciejowice (MAHTS-YAY-OH-VEE-TSAY).

question.leadin: Answer the following questions about anti-communist unrest in Poland.
question.text: Solidarity's leader at the 1981 Gdansk shipyards protests was this man, who later became the first democratically elected president of Poland after the dissolution of the Soviet Union.
question.clue: The KOR ("K-O-R") was a predecessor to an organization led by this man, which formed a coalition government with the PUWP.

swap.leadin: After World War II, this animal spent his days at Edinburgh Zoo, sometimes getting tossed cigars from fellow veterans.
swap.text: Name this Syrian Brown Bear who fought with the Polish II Corps and famously carried 100 pound cases of artillery across the battlefield.
swap.clue: This adorable bear was purchased by Polish soldiers during World War II, being taught to move artillery and apparently enjoying eating cigarettes. His name is a diminutive for "joyful warrior."

question.leadin: Raging from 1733 to 1738, it was sparked by the death of Augustus the Strong and the competition between sjems to name an heir.
question.text: Name this conflict, ended by the Treaty of Vienna, which put Frederick Augustus on the throne of the European kingdom that had once been joined with Lithuania in the Union of Lublin.
question.clue: The person who led the Confederation of Dzikow had previously held the job in question under Swedish domination and was the father-in-law of Louis XV.

swap.text: It was founded by Wadyslaw II, who married Jadigwa, and continued through several Sigismunds until the country fell under the rule of the French Valois. For 15 points, name this Polish royal house of the fourteenth through sixteenth centuries.
swap.clue: This dynasty, first established when a certain king married Queen Jadwiga. It held power in a country long united with Poland.

question.text: The Khmelnytsky Uprising initiated this historical period, in which Russia and Sweden repeatedly invaded Poland. Its name comes from the title of a Henryk Sienkiewicz ["SHEN-kyay-veech"] novel.
question.clue: Key precipitating factors of this period include the increased power of the nobility due to Sarmatism and Golden Liberty system, and it saw secondary conflicts like the Second Northern War.

swap.text: Under the liberum veto rule, any noble could veto an act of the Sejm, the parliament of this country. The Union of Lublin united this country with Lithuania and it was later partitioned three times in the 18th century.
swap.clue: Rulers of this kingdom agreed to a set of "articles" named after Henry of Valois, its first elected king.

question.text: Victims of Operation Vistula were relocated to the Recovered Territories gained by Poland after World War II, one of which was this "free city" on a namesake corridor, whose post office was the site of a siege during the 1939 Nazi invasion.
question.clue: An earlier siege of this city in 1577 ended inconclusively, with this city gaining an independent charter from Stefan Bathory in exchange for supporting his claim to the throne of Poland and paying a huge ransom.

swap.leadin: In 1943, the Baedeker Guide published its guide to this place, where a historian noted that a "shed where dozens of corpses lie awaiting burial is particularly popular" among tourists.
swap.text: Name this place, many of whose residents were sent to Treblinka. After an unsuccessful Jewish uprising, this area of the Polish capital was destroyed.
swap.clue: The Armia Krajowa largely failed to aid an insurrection partially led by Mordecai Anielewicz in this place, which was documented in a report named for the SS officer who suppressed it, Jurgen Stroop.

question.text: This Grand Duke of Lithuania and later King of Poland converted the last pagan state in Europe, Lithuania, to Christianity, and then laid the smack-down on the Teutonic Knights at the First Battle of Tannenberg in 1410.
question.answerHtml: Wladyslaw II (accept Jogaila or Jagiello as family name)

swap.leadin: After this battle, the victors placed the head of Henry II the Pious on a spear and paraded it through nearby villages, and also filled nine sacks with the severed ears of their fallen enemies.
swap.text: Name this 1241 clash that, along with the Battle of Mohi in Hungary two days later, marks the farthest extent of Mongol expansion into Europe. Despite their victory, the Mongols returned east upon news of Ogedei's death.
swap.answerHtml: Battle of Legnica [or Battle of Liegnitz; or Battle of Wahlstatt]

question.text: In 1000 CE, Boleslaw and Otto III of the Holy Roman Empire agreed to establish the first Polish archbishopric at a congress in this Piast capital city, where Saint Adalbert was buried until the corpse was transferred to St. Vitus Cathedral.

swap.leadin: It was led by Mordecai Anielewicz, a member of the ZOB.
swap.text: This is what uprising in the spring of 1943, in which the inhabitants of the namesake location in Poland unsuccessfully attempted to resist Nazi mass deportation to Treblinka.
swap.clue: This event was meant to coincide with Operation Bagration, but the Red Army suddenly halted its advance and refused to lend support once it began.

question.text: This Polish king brought stability through an alliance with Austria. He was forced to give right-bank Ukraine up to the Ottomans, but he took his revenge when he broke the Siege of Vienna in 1683.
question.answerHtml: Jan III Sobieski (either Jan III or Jan Sobieski acceptable)
question.clue: His victory at Chocim coincided with the death of his predecessor Michael I, allowing him to take power.

swap.leadin: Sadly for this man, he ordered his victorious forces not to destroy the enemy army at the battle of Stegeborg to reduce the massacre.
swap.text: Name this Catholic who was then soundly defeated at the battle of Stangebro by his uncle Duke Charles, who stripped him of one of his thrones in 1599, though he continued to rule Poland for quite a while.
swap.answerHtml: Sigismund III Vasa [or Sigismund of Sweden; prompt on partial answers]
swap.clue: This ruler and his cousin signed a peace treaty at Altmark that was extended by this ruler's son at Stuhmsdorf.
